descripcion_es: I/me, he/him, she/her…: when to use each form.
resumen: Subject pronouns (I, he, she…) do the action and go before the verb; object pronouns (me, him, her…) receive it and go after the verb or after a preposition. In English the subject is never left out.

explicacion.texto: In Spanish the subject can be left out because the verb already shows the person (es: “vivo en Madrid”); in English it is compulsory: I live in Madrid. For things, animals and situations you use it, also as an empty subject: It's raining, It's late.

items: After a preposition you always use the object pronoun: with me, for them, between us.
In short informal answers: Who's there? It's me. Who wants tea? Me!
Object pronouns go after the verb, not before it as in Spanish: I see her (es: “la veo”).

ejemplos.frase: I met Sara yesterday and invited her to dinner.
ejemplos.traduccion: Ayer vi a Sara y la invité a cenar.

ejemplos.frase: These biscuits are good. Try them!
He's my neighbour, but I don't know him well.
ejemplos.traduccion: Es mi vecino, pero no lo conozco bien.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: Is my brother. Is a doctor.
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: He's my brother. He's a doctor.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: The subject cannot be left out.
The object pronoun goes after the verb.
After a preposition you use the object pronoun.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: Me and Juan go to the gym.
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: Juan and I go to the gym.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: As a subject you use I; for politeness it goes last.

ejercicios.frase: Where is Tom? I can't see ___.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the card's table: the object form of he (subject) is him. Tom is a man and here he is the object of the verb see, so it is him, after the verb. In Spanish the pronoun goes before the verb (“lo veo”), but in English the object always follows the verb.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Tom is he, and as an object: him.

errores_previstos.explicacion: He is a subject pronoun; as the object of the verb see you need him.
His is a possessive; for the object you use him.
It is used for things and animals; for a person (Tom) it is him.

ejercicios.frase: I love these songs. I listen to ___ every day.
ejercicios.explicacion: The card's rule says that after a preposition you always use the object pronoun. Listen to has the preposition to, and what you listen to is these songs, plural, which corresponds to they. Its object form is them. In Spanish “las escucho” goes before the verb, but in English it goes after the preposition: listen to them.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: These songs is they, and as an object: them.
ejercicios.traduccion: Me encantan estas canciones. Las escucho todos los días.

errores_previstos.explicacion: They is a subject; after the preposition to comes the object form, them.
These songs is plural: them, not it.
Their is a possessive; as an object it is them.

ejercicios.frase: My mother phones ___ every Sunday. We always talk for an hour.
ejercicios.explicacion: According to the card's table, we (subject) becomes us when it is an object. The clue is the second sentence, We always talk, which shows that the people being called are us. My mother is the one who calls (subject) and we receive the call (object), so it is us after phones.
ejercicios.traduccion: Mi madre nos llama todos los domingos. Siempre hablamos una hora.

errores_previstos.explicacion: We is the subject form; as the object of phones you need us.
Our is a possessive; as an object it is us.
The reflexive is only used if subject and object are the same; here it is the mother who calls: us.

ejercicios.frase: Laura is my friend. ___ works in a bookshop.
ejercicios.explicacion: The card reminds you that in English the subject is never left out, even though in Spanish we just say “trabaja”. Laura is a woman and does the action of works, so you need the subject pronoun she. It has a capital letter because it is at the beginning of the sentence. A bookshop is a shop that sells books (es: librería), not a library (es: biblioteca).
ejercicios.traduccion: Laura es mi amiga. Trabaja en una librería.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Her is an object or a possessive; as the subject of works you need She.
Laura is a woman: She.
It is for things and animals; for a person it is She.

glosario.definicion_l: a shop where books are sold

ejercicios.frase: What time is it? ___ is half past six.
ejercicios.explicacion: The card explains that it works as an empty subject for the time, the weather and other situations: It's raining, It's late. In Spanish we say “son las seis y media” with no subject, but in English you need It is (It's) half past six. Half past six means thirty minutes after six o'clock.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: The time is given with it as the subject.
ejercicios.traduccion: ¿Qué hora es? Son las seis y media.

errores_previstos.explicacion: A calque of Spanish “son las”: the time is always given with singular it.
For the time you use the empty subject it, not this.
There is is used to say that something exists; the time takes It is.

ejercicios.explicacion: According to the card's table, I (subject) becomes me when it is an object. Here the one who helps is you and the one who receives the help is me, so after the verb help it is me. In Spanish the pronoun is attached to the verb (“ayudarme”), but in English it is separate and goes after it.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Object of the verb help: me.

por_opcion.I: I is the subject form; after the verb help you need the object, me.
por_opcion.me: Correct: first person singular object pronoun.
por_opcion.my: My is a possessive and needs a noun after it (my bag).

ejercicios.explicacion: The card states that after a preposition you always use the object pronoun. For is a preposition, so it is her. Note that her works both as an object (for her) and as a possessive (her letter); here it is an object because no noun follows it.

por_opcion.she: She is a subject pronoun; after the preposition for comes the object form.
por_opcion.her: Correct: object pronoun after the preposition for.
por_opcion.hers: Hers is a possessive pronoun (es: “suya”): This letter is hers would mean that the letter belongs to her, and it does not go after for.

ejercicios.explicacion: The card reminds you that the subject pronoun goes before the verb. The gap is the subject of are, so you need they. Them would be an object and their is a possessive that requires a noun after it. In Spanish we could just say “son mis mejores amigos”, but in English the subject is compulsory.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Subject of the verb are: they.

por_opcion.Them: Them is an object pronoun; it cannot be the subject of are.
por_opcion.They: Correct: subject pronoun for the plural.
por_opcion.Their: Their is a possessive and needs a noun after it (their friends).

ejercicios.enunciado: Replace the keys with a pronoun.
ejercicios.explicacion: The rule in the card's table says that the object form of they is them. The keys is plural and is the object of find, so it is replaced by them, which stays after the verb. In Spanish the pronoun goes before the verb (“no las encuentro”), but in English the order does not change when you replace it: I can't find them.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: The keys is plural and an object: them.

errores_previstos.explicacion: The keys is plural: them, not it.
A calque of Spanish word order: the object goes after the verb, find them.
They is a subject; as an object you need them.

ejercicios.enunciado: Replace my sister with a pronoun.
ejercicios.explicacion: The card's table shows that she becomes her as an object. My sister is the object of visit, so it is changed to her, in the same place, after the verb. The adverb often stays before the verb, as with adverbs of frequency.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: My sister as an object: her.
ejercicios.traduccion: Visito a menudo a mi hermana. (La visito a menudo.)

errores_previstos.explicacion: She is the subject form; as an object you need her.
The object goes after the verb: visit her.
It is for things; for a person, my sister, it is her.

ejercicios.explicacion: The card explains that in English the subject is compulsory and that it works as an empty subject for the time and situations such as It's late. In Spanish “es muy tarde” has no subject, and the calque leaves the sentence without one. You must add It at the beginning: It is very late or It's very late.

errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the uncorrected sentence: the empty subject it is missing.
For the time or the moment you use the empty subject it, not this.
That would be a question; in a statement, the subject goes first: It is very late.

ejercicios.frase: Come with we to the beach!
respuestas: Come with us to the beach!
ejercicios.explicacion: According to the card, after a preposition you always use the object pronoun. With is a preposition, so we (subject) must be changed to us (object). In Spanish “con nosotros” uses the same form as the subject, which is why learners tend to say with we.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: After with comes the object pronoun us.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Come with we to the beach!
errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the uncorrected sentence: after with it is us.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Come with our to the beach!
errores_previstos.explicacion: Our is a possessive and needs a noun; after with it is us.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Come with ourselves to the beach!
errores_previstos.explicacion: The reflexive does not fit here: the object of the preposition is simply us.

ejercicios.explicacion: The card reminds you that the subject pronoun goes before the verb. The gap is the subject of is, so him (object) must be replaced by he. The contraction He's my cousin is also correct. Cousin is the child of your uncle or aunt (es: primo or prima); it is not used for a nephew (es: sobrino).
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: As a subject you use he.

errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the uncorrected sentence: as a subject you use he.
His is a possessive; the subject of is must be he.
In English the subject cannot be left out: He is my cousin.

respuestas: I don't know them very well
ejercicios.explicacion: The card gives the basic order: subject + verb + object, and the adverb after it. The subject is I, the negative verb don't know, the object them, and very well closes the sentence. In Spanish the pronoun goes before the verb (“no los conozco”), but in English it goes after, and very well is not placed between the verb and the object.

errores_previstos.respuesta: I don't them know very well
errores_previstos.explicacion: A calque of Spanish: the object them goes after the verb know.

errores_previstos.respuesta: I don't know very well them
errores_previstos.explicacion: The adverb is not placed between the verb and the object: know them very well.

descripcion_larga_es: Subject personal pronouns (I, he, she…) and object personal pronouns (me, him, her…) let you avoid repeating names. In English the subject is compulsory, even it for the time or the weather, and the object pronoun goes after the verb or the preposition. Spanish speakers find it hard not to leave out the subject (Is late), not to put the object first and to use me or us after a preposition.

contexto.que_es: They are the words that replace a person or thing already mentioned. There are two sets: subject pronouns (I, you, he, she, it, we, they), which do the action, and object pronouns (me, you, him, her, it, us, them), which receive it or go after a preposition.
contexto.por_que_importa: They appear in almost every sentence, so a mistake here is repeated constantly. Leaving out the subject or using the wrong form (Him is my cousin, with we) sounds very foreign and can even make it unclear who you are talking about. Using it correctly as an empty subject is key for the time, the weather and many evaluations (It's important that…).
contexto.cuando_se_usa: Subject pronouns go before the verb in every clause with a conjugated verb; object pronouns go after the verb (I see her), after a preposition (for them) and in short answers (It's me). Spanish speakers, used to leaving out the subject and placing the object before the verb (“la veo”), tend to write Is late or to hesitate over word order.
